title: Containers, pods, deployments

story: It is 3 in the morning. The broker, the service that holds our GitHub credentials and pushes Nova's commits, runs as two copies on two machines in our internal cluster. AWS needs one of those machines back, so the machine disappears, and one copy of the broker disappears with it. Nobody is awake.

At 3:01 Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, finishes a step on RH-1234 and pushes a checkpoint commit through the broker. The push works. In the morning there is no alert, no ticket and nothing in Slack, and the broker is running as two copies again, one of them on a machine that did not exist last night. On your laptop, a container that dies stays dead until you type docker run again, so somebody must have done that here.
hook.question: Who brought the broker back at 3 in the morning, and how did Nova still find it?

read.h: You write down what should be true
p: In p1-8 you built an image for a Node service and ran it with docker run. A running image is a container: one process with its own files and its own network. On your laptop you are the one who starts it, and you are the one who starts it again when it stops. That works for one laptop, but not for a service that must answer at 3 in the morning on machines that come and go.

Kubernetes changes the question you answer. You do not say "start this container on that machine". You write down what should be true, for example "two copies of the broker image should be running", and you hand that to the cluster. A cluster is a group of machines, called nodes, plus a control plane, which is the part that stores what you asked for and keeps comparing it with what is really running. When the two differ, the control plane acts until they match again. People call what you wrote the desired state, and the endless compare-and-fix the control loop. Nobody restarted the broker last night: the control loop saw one copy where you asked for two, and started another.

Our cluster for internal tools is called inf-rhinohealth, or inf for short. It is Amazon EKS, which is Kubernetes run by AWS, and it already runs tools like Vault (our secret store), n8n (an older workflow tool), Nexus (our package mirror) and VictoriaMetrics (where our metrics are stored). The agent platform's services live there too: the LLM gateway, the broker, the orchestrator worker, the Slack app and our own Temporal. They run on inf because they hold credentials, and credentials never go to the sandbox VMs where the agents work. Those VMs are not in this cluster at all; they are EC2 machines in a separate AWS account. The nodes of inf are cheap Spot machines that AWS can take back, which is exactly what happened at 3 in the morning.

read.h: A pod is replaced, never repaired
p: Kubernetes never runs a bare container. It runs a pod, which is one or more containers that share one IP address. Almost all of our pods hold exactly one container, so for now you can read "pod" as "one running copy of the service". A pod is never repaired. When its node disappears or its process crashes for good, that pod is gone, and a new pod with a new random name and a new IP address takes its place.

So you do not create pods yourself. You create a Deployment, which says which image to run and how many copies, called replicas, to keep. The Deployment carries a template, a recipe that every new pod is stamped from, and a selector, which says which pods count as its own. Below is the shape of the broker's Deployment, shortened. You will rarely type this file, because our Terraform and Helm code produces it, but you need to read it.

code.text:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: broker
  namespace: ai-agents
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: broker
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: broker
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: broker
          image: 123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/ai-agents-broker@sha256:4b1e…
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /health, port: 8080 }
          securityContext:
            runAsUser: 10001
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true

notes.text: The namespace, a folder for objects in the cluster. All our agent services share the one called ai-agents.
The desired state: two copies. Lose one and the control loop starts another; there is no autoscaling on inf, so the number stays fixed.
The selector: every pod with the label app=broker belongs to this Deployment and counts towards the two.
Everything under template is the pod recipe. A replacement pod gets exactly this, and nothing you changed by hand on the old one.
The image is pinned by digest, the hash of its content, as you saw in p1-8. A tag could later point at different bytes; a digest cannot.
A pod receives calls only after GET /health answers. Until then it exists but is not "ready".

deeper.h: Go deeper: what happens when you change the image
p: When the recipe changes, for example a new image digest, the Deployment does a rolling update: it starts one new pod, waits until it is ready, and only then removes an old one, and so on until every pod runs the new recipe. So a bad image does not take the service down. In the lab cluster, a Deployment pointed at an image tag that does not exist got one new pod stuck in ErrImagePull, while the three old pods stayed Running and kept answering.

kubectl rollout undo deployment/broker then goes back to the previous recipe. On inf you would not run that by hand, because the Terraform unit would put the bad digest back on the next apply; you revert the digest in the unit instead, and the next lesson shows that path.

read.h: A Service is the name that stays
p: Now the second half of the story. The orchestrator calls the broker hundreds of times a day. If its config held a pod's IP address, last night's replacement would have broken every call, because the new pod got a new address. So nobody writes down a pod's name or IP. Instead there is a Service: a stable name in front of whichever pods match a label at this moment. When a call arrives, the Service sends it to one of the ready pods.

Inside the cluster that name is a DNS name, broker.ai-agents, which is short for broker.ai-agents.svc.cluster.local: the Service name, then the namespace. That is the address in the orchestrator's config, and that is why Nova's 3:01 push still worked. The sandbox VMs reach the broker another way, through a private network path you will meet in p5-4.

code.file: the Service next to the broker's Deployment
code.text:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: broker
  namespace: ai-agents
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: broker
  ports:
    - port: 8080
      targetPort: 8080

notes.text: With the namespace on line 5, this gives the DNS name broker.ai-agents.
ClusterIP means reachable from inside the cluster only. Nothing on the internet can call it.
The same label as the Deployment's pods. This label is the whole link between the Service and the pods: get it wrong and the Service points at nothing.
The port the container listens on. Callers use port, the Service forwards to targetPort.

p: Most of the time you will read the cluster, not change it, because every change to inf arrives as a Terraform pull request that a person applies. Five commands answer almost every question. Each one takes -n and a namespace; if you forget it, kubectl looks in the namespace called default, finds nothing, and you will think your pods are gone.

The first command matters most. kubectl talks to whichever cluster its current context points at, and on a work laptop that can be a real product cluster. So always check the context first. In the lab you will go one step further and give kubectl a separate key file that only knows your laptop cluster, so a mistake there can never reach anything real.

code.text:
kubectl config current-context
kubectl -n ai-agents get pods
kubectl -n ai-agents describe pod broker-6f9c4d79c8-qkjbl
kubectl -n ai-agents logs deploy/broker --tail=50
kubectl -n ai-agents get deploy,svc

notes.text: Which cluster am I talking to? Run it before anything else.
READY 1/1 and STATUS Running are good. CrashLoopBackOff means the process keeps exiting; ImagePullBackOff means the image or digest is wrong.
The Events list at the bottom is where Kubernetes explains why a pod is waiting or crashing.
deploy/broker means "any pod of this Deployment", so you never need the random pod name.

lab.title: A Deployment that heals itself
needs: Docker Desktop running, with about 1 GB of memory free
lab.goal: Run a small Kubernetes cluster in Docker, give it a Deployment and a Service, delete a pod, and watch the cluster bring it back while the name keeps working.

guess.q: The Deployment broker asks for 2 replicas, and both pods are running. You delete one of them by name. What does kubectl get pods show a few seconds later?

options.text: One pod, because you deleted the other one.
options.why: That is what docker rm would do. Here the control loop sees one pod where the Deployment asks for two, and starts another.

options.text: Two pods with the same names as before, because Kubernetes restarted the deleted one.
options.why: A deleted pod is never brought back. A new pod is made from the template, with a new random name and a new IP.

options.text: Two pods: the one you did not touch, and a new one with a new name and an age of a few seconds.
options.why: The Deployment keeps the count, not the pods. The replacement is a fresh pod stamped from the same recipe.

follow.say: Start a small Kubernetes cluster inside one Docker container. k3s is a light Kubernetes made for small machines, and this one command gives you a real control plane and one node called academy.
follow.do: docker run -d --name academy --hostname academy --privileged -p 6443:6443 rancher/k3s:v1.33.5-k3s1 server --disable=traefik --disable=metrics-server
follow.see:
Unable to find image 'rancher/k3s:v1.33.5-k3s1' locally
v1.33.5-k3s1: Pulling from rancher/k3s
…
Status: Downloaded newer image for rancher/k3s:v1.33.5-k3s1
7f507baea574b1673950eef750a394c3396ef7b1b14b08a77ccd970cab428b8c

follow.say: Copy the cluster's key file out of the container and point kubectl at it for this terminal only. Your normal kubectl settings stay untouched, so nothing you do here can reach a real cluster. Wait about 20 seconds after the last step before you run this.
follow.do: docker cp academy:/etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml ~/academy-k3s.yaml && export KUBECONFIG=~/academy-k3s.yaml && kubectl config current-context && kubectl get nodes
follow.see:
default
NAME      STATUS   ROLES                  AGE   VERSION
academy   Ready    control-plane,master   41s   v1.33.5+k3s1

follow.say: Create the namespace and a Deployment with two replicas. nginx plays the part of the broker, because it is a small web server that answers on port 80.
follow.do: kubectl create namespace ai-agents && kubectl -n ai-agents create deployment broker --image=nginx:1.27 --replicas=2

follow.say: Look at the two pods. Note their names and their IP addresses, because you are about to lose one.
follow.see:
NAME                      READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE   IP          NODE
broker-6f9c4d79c8-mmqmq   1/1     Running   0          26s   10.42.0.4   academy
broker-6f9c4d79c8-qkjbl   1/1     Running   0          25s   10.42.0.5   academy

follow.say: Delete one pod, the way a disappearing node would, and look again straight away. Use one of your own pod names.
follow.do: kubectl -n ai-agents delete pod broker-6f9c4d79c8-mmqmq && kubectl -n ai-agents get pods -o wide
follow.see:
pod "broker-6f9c4d79c8-mmqmq" deleted
NAME                      READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE   IP          NODE
broker-6f9c4d79c8-cpxzw   1/1     Running   0          1s    10.42.0.6   academy
broker-6f9c4d79c8-qkjbl   1/1     Running   0          31s   10.42.0.5   academy

follow.say: Put a Service in front of the pods, then call it by name from a throwaway pod inside the cluster, which is what the orchestrator does when it calls the broker.
follow.do: kubectl -n ai-agents expose deployment broker --port=80 && kubectl -n ai-agents run probe --rm -i --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl:8.11.1 -- curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://broker.ai-agents

follow.say: Ask the Service which pods it is sending calls to right now. These are the IPs of the two live pods, including the new one.
follow.do: kubectl -n ai-agents describe service broker | grep -E 'Selector|Endpoints'

lab.build: Add the orchestrator next to the broker, this time from a file, the way Terraform and Helm will give it to the cluster. Let kubectl write the starting YAML for you: kubectl -n ai-agents create deployment orchestrator --image=nginx:1.27 --replicas=1 --dry-run=client -o yaml > orchestrator.yaml. Open the file, change replicas to 2, and run kubectl apply -f orchestrator.yaml. Then prove three things on your own: both orchestrator pods are Running, deleting one of them brings a new one with a new name, and an orchestrator pod reaches the broker by its Service name: kubectl -n ai-agents exec deploy/orchestrator -- curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://broker prints 200.
checks: kubectl config current-context prints default, and kubectl get nodes shows one node called academy (your laptop cluster, not a real one)
After you delete a broker pod, kubectl -n ai-agents get pods still shows two broker pods, one with a new name and an age of a few seconds
The probe pod prints 200 for http://broker.ai-agents
kubectl -n ai-agents get deploy shows broker 2/2 and orchestrator 2/2
kubectl -n ai-agents exec deploy/orchestrator -- curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' http://broker prints 200

solution.text:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  labels:
    app: orchestrator
  name: orchestrator
  namespace: ai-agents
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: orchestrator
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: orchestrator
    spec:
      containers:
      - image: nginx:1.27
        name: nginx

lab.fix: A teammate renamed some labels and changed the broker Service's selector to match a new label name. Do the same with kubectl -n ai-agents set selector service broker app=brokr, then call it again with the probe pod: it now prints 000 instead of 200, although both broker pods are still Running. Find out why with kubectl -n ai-agents describe service broker (look at Selector and Endpoints) and kubectl -n ai-agents get pods --show-labels, then repair it with one command so the probe prints 200 again.
explain: Nobody ran a restart command, yet a deleted pod came back. What compared what, and what did it do about the difference?
Why does the orchestrator's config hold broker.ai-agents and never a pod name or an IP address?
In the broken Service, the pods were healthy but every call failed. What is the only link between a Service and its pods?
lab.done: You deleted a pod and the Deployment replaced it with a new name and IP, the Service name kept working, and when you are finished with p5 you remove the cluster with docker rm -f academy and delete ~/academy-k3s.yaml.

check.q: A broker pod keeps crashing because of a wrong setting in its environment. A teammate wants to log in to the pod, fix the file and restart the process. Why does that not work on Kubernetes?

options.text: Because pods have no shell, so you cannot log in to them at all
options.why: Many pods do have a shell, and kubectl exec can open it. The problem is what happens to your change afterwards.

options.text: Because the next replacement pod is stamped from the Deployment's template, so a change made inside one pod disappears with that pod
options.why: Pods are replaced, never repaired. The fix belongs in the recipe, which on inf means the Terraform unit, so every future pod gets it.

options.text: Because Kubernetes forbids changes to running pods and rolls them back at once
options.why: Nothing watches the files inside a pod. The change would even work for a while, until the pod is replaced and the fix is lost.

check.q: Which address should the orchestrator use to call the broker?

options.text: The IP address of a broker pod, from kubectl get pods -o wide
options.why: That address belongs to one pod and is gone when the pod is replaced, as it was at 3 in the morning.
The Service name stays the same while pods come and go, and it sends each call to a ready pod.

options.text: The node's IP address, because nodes live longer than pods
options.why: On inf the nodes are Spot machines that AWS can take back, so they come and go too, and a pod can move to any node.

check.q: You asked for 2 replicas. A node disappears and takes one pod with it. What brings the count back to 2?

options.text: The control loop, which compares the desired state with what is running and starts a pod from the template
options.why: That compare-and-fix is the core of Kubernetes. It works the same at 3 in the morning as at noon, with nobody awake.

options.text: An alert that wakes the on-call person, who runs kubectl to start a pod
options.why: No person is needed. An alert may still be useful, for example when pods keep crashing, but it is not what restores the count.

options.text: Docker on the node, which restarts containers that stop
options.why: The node itself is gone, so nothing on it can help. The new pod is started on a different node by the control plane.

p: Every agent service on inf is a Deployment plus a Service in the ai-agents namespace, produced by one shared Helm chart, modules/ai-agents-service, so the gateway, the broker, the orchestrator worker and the Slack app all look alike. Replica counts are fixed numbers, because KEDA, the tool that would scale them automatically, is off on inf: the gateway and the broker run 2, the orchestrator worker 2, the Slack app 1. Pods run as user 10001 with a read-only root filesystem and the image pinned by digest.

Two services break the pattern on purpose. The brain bot and the Slack app use Slack's Socket Mode, which means they dial out to Slack and nobody dials in, so the brain bot has no Service at all. And our Temporal is the upstream Temporal chart rather than our own, but it renders the same kinds of objects you met here.

tickets.why: The first agent service on inf, the LLM gateway, and the shared chart every later service reuses.
The broker, the orchestrator worker and the Slack app as Deployments with fixed replicas and digest-pinned images.
Our own Temporal on inf: the upstream chart's Deployments and a ClusterIP frontend Service.
The brain bot: one replica and no Service, because Socket Mode only dials out.

words.plain: One running copy of a service: one or more containers sharing an IP. It is replaced, never repaired.
Says which image to run and how many pods to keep, and replaces pods that disappear.
A stable name in front of whichever pods carry a certain label right now.
A folder for objects in a cluster. Our agent services share the one called ai-agents.
The control plane's endless compare-and-fix between what you asked for and what is running.
Our internal Kubernetes cluster (Amazon EKS), where internal tools and the agent services run.

review.q: Draw the broker on inf from memory: the Deployment, its pods, the Service and the orchestrator calling it. Mark the one label that ties them together.
review.a: A Deployment broker with replicas 2 and a template labelled app=broker; two pods with that label; a Service broker selecting app=broker; the orchestrator calling broker.ai-agents.

review.q: A pod shows STATUS ImagePullBackOff after a deploy. What does it mean, and where do you fix it?
review.a: The node could not download the image, usually a wrong digest or no access to the registry. Fix the image in the recipe (the Terraform unit), not in the pod.

review.q: Why do the sandbox VMs not run on inf, while the broker does?
review.a: The broker holds credentials, so it runs in the cluster we control. The VMs run untrusted work and hold no keys, so they live in a separate AWS account and reach inf only through a narrow private path.

remember: You write down what should be true, a Deployment and a Service; the cluster replaces pods to keep it true, and callers only ever use the Service's name.
